en: The Dharma of the Eight Precepts of Fasting, compiled by the Śramaṇa Hongzan of Baoxianglin Monastery in Guangzhou while residing in Jiqiu.
When the Tathāgata governed the world, his primary purpose was to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings; yet, the faculties and natures of these beings differ.

Therefore, various methods were established in the teachings. Although the teachings are not uniform, they do not go beyond the Three Trainings—namely, morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
While there are many gateways for concentration and wisdom, morality is categorized into seven groups.

For those who have left the household life, a *bhikṣu* receives and upholds the two hundred and fifty major precepts, a *bhikṣuṇī* maintains three hundred and forty-eight precepts, and a *śikṣamāṇā*...
They study these six dharmas. Both śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs uphold the ten precepts. For laypeople, there are the upāsakas and upāsikās;
thus, the precepts open two gates: first, the five precepts to be observed for the duration of one’s life;

second, the eight precepts to be observed on the six fast days, or the ten fast days, or according to one’s own inclination—observing them whenever one has leisure. Although the precepts are thus described...
The merit and benefits obtained in a single day and night are beyond the comprehension of ordinary beings.
Just as a *maṇi* jewel, though small in size, surpasses all other treasures, so too is this wholesome benefit. There are two kinds of people who abandon it and do not practice it:
first, those who do not believe in the causes and effects of good and evil across the three periods of time; and second, those who, being Confucians, do not cultivate virtue.

Regarding the Five Constant Virtues: it would be better to believe that the Tathāgata appeared in the world to bestow the Five Precepts. Because of these [two types of people], the path to the human and celestial realms is cut off, and they have no share in the fruits of the Way.

The first type is stubbornly ignorant and lacks understanding; they do not recognize the duties of ruler and subject, father and son, nor do they know filial piety, fraternal respect, loyalty, or good faith.
They know only eating and resting, being no different from beasts. How could they understand the transformation toward goodness? These two kinds of people have obtained a human body in vain. First.

In this life, there is no good to be recorded; one acts according to one's whims and does not cultivate what is right. Once the fruits of karma manifest before one, how can one regret it when it is too late?
Therefore, those who possess wisdom should quickly accept and uphold [the precepts]. The *Āgama Sūtra* states:

The Buddha said, "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to obtain the Eightfold Observance (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*), to leave behind all sufferings, to exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*), and to enter the city of Nirvāṇa..."
One should seek skillful means to accomplish these eight precepts of the fast. The positions of honor among humans are not to be considered noble;
the bliss of the heavens is beyond measure. Those who wish to seek unsurpassed merit should seek this fast.

Those who wish to be born in the heavens of the six realms of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm should observe this fast. Those who wish to seek [mastery over] one direction, two directions, or three...
As for the four directions, the celestial kings and those in the position of a wheel-turning sage king shall likewise obtain their vows.
Those who seek the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, or the Buddha—all shall fulfill their aspirations. That I have now achieved [this] is entirely due to upholding the precepts;

through the eightfold fast and the ten wholesome actions, there is no vow that is not obtained. If one receives the eightfold abstinence, one must first repent of prior transgressions, and only then receive it.
Regarding the precepts, one should give rise to a sense of shame and remorse, and with a sincere and earnest heart, speak as follows:
"I, [Name], from beginningless birth and death until this very day, have committed unwholesome deeds of body—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct;
unwholesome deeds of speech—falsehood, frivolous talk, divisive speech, and harsh words; and unwholesome deeds of mind—covetousness and anger."
Out of anger, delusion, and false views, and lacking faith in cause and effect, one has committed these ten unwholesome offenses.
Now, before the Triple Gem of the ten directions, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the holy assemblies of the Three Vehicles, and the teachers and monks present here, I seek compassion and repent.
Having performed this repentance, the instructor says:

I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha for one day and one night, as a lay follower (*upāsaka*) of pure conduct (for a woman, one should say *upāsikā*).
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is my World-Honored One. (Having recited this three times, one then receives the three precepts.)
I, [Name], have taken refuge in the Buddha; I have taken refuge in the Dharma; I have taken refuge in the Saṃgha. For one day and one night, may I be a lay follower (*upāsaka*) of pure conduct.
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is my World-Honored One. (Having recited this three times, next follows the ritual for receiving the precepts.)
Just as all Buddhas throughout their lives refrain from taking life, so shall I, [name], refrain from taking life for one day and one night.
Just as all Buddhas throughout their lives refrain from taking what is not given, so shall I, [name], refrain from taking what is not given for one day and one night.
Just as all Buddhas throughout their lives refrain from sexual misconduct, so shall I, [name], refrain from sexual misconduct for one day and one night.
Just as all Buddhas throughout their lives refrain from false speech, so shall I, [name], refrain from false speech for one day and one night.
Just as all Buddhas throughout their lives did not drink alcohol, so I, [name], for one day and one night shall not drink alcohol.
Just as all Buddhas throughout their lives did not wear garlands of fragrant flowers nor anoint their bodies with perfumes, so I, [name],
for one day and one night shall not wear garlands of fragrant flowers nor anoint my body with perfumes.
Just as all Buddhas throughout their lives did not engage in singing, dancing, or performing music, nor went to listen to or watch such performances;
so may I, [Name], for one day and one night, refrain from singing, dancing, or performing music, and refrain from going to watch or listen to them.
Just as all Buddhas, for the duration of their lives, did not sit upon high, wide, or large beds, so shall I, [name], for one day and one night, not sit upon a high, wide, or large bed.
Just as all Buddhas, for the duration of their lives, did not eat at improper times, so shall I, [name], for one day and one night, not eat at an improper time.
The Sūtra says: "Having conferred [the precepts] in the sequence above, one should instruct them to make a vow. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra says: "One should make this vow, saying:
'I, [Name], having received and practiced the eight precepts, follow and learn from all Buddhas; this is called upoṣadha (poṣadha).

I vow to maintain this merit so as not to fall into the three evil realms or the eight difficulties. Furthermore, I do not seek the pleasures of a wheel-turning monarch, a Brahmā king, or the world at large. I vow to sever all afflictions.'"
One shall attain all-knowledge and accomplish the Buddha-way. (If one wishes to simultaneously repay the four debts of gratitude and seek rebirth in a Pure Land, one should make a vow as follows:)
By the merit of these eight precepts of the fast, I now repay the four debts of gratitude in their entirety and provide sustenance for all beings in the three realms of existence;
may I universally share this with all sentient beings so that we may be reborn together in the Pure Land.
These eight precepts of abstinence are also called the eightfold precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*), and are further termed the eight dharmas for nurturing merit.
Of these, the first eight are called the "precepts of abstinence" (*gati-śīla*), while the final one—refraining from eating at improper times—is called "fasting" (*upavāsa*).

Because the term "fasting" is combined with the "precepts of abstinence," they are collectively referred to as the "eightfold precepts of abstinence and fasting. "Abstinence" (*gati*) means to close off the eight evils so that no transgressions arise; this constitutes the fast.

"Zhai" (齋) means "equilibrium. It refers to restraining the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), remaining unstained by the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), completely severing all evils, and fully cultivating all virtues;
therefore, it is called *zhāi* (齋). The *Mahā-upāya-kauśalya-sūtra* states:

Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying, "The eight precepts of fasting (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*), together with the abstention from eating after midday, constitute nine dharmas. Why is it named after only eight matters? The Buddha said: "Fasting..."
The essence of this dharma consists of not eating after midday. Eight matters assist in establishing the substance of the fast, supporting one another;
thus it is called the "Eight-Limbed Fast Dharma" (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa). For this reason, it is called the "Eight Precepts" (aṣṭa-śīla) and not nine. Regarding "not killing":
from the smallest insect upward, for any living being, one must not intentionally kill. Regarding "not stealing": even down to a single needle...
First, the precept of abstaining from taking what is not given: he does not take anything that has not been offered to him. Second, the precept of abstaining from sexual misconduct:

regarding all men and women in the world, as well as his own wife or concubines, he completely refrains from them for one day and one night. Third, the precept of abstaining from false speech: there are four kinds of false speech.
This refers to lying, frivolous speech, slander, and harsh speech; in short, whatever is inconsistent with one's mind and mouth is all termed lying.
Regarding "not drinking alcohol": this means that anything fermented from the five grains, flowers, or fruits that is capable of intoxicating a person must not be drunk.
Regarding "not wearing fragrant flower garlands or anointing the body with perfumes": this means that one must not use various flowers [for such purposes].
Stringing them together as garlands, using fragrant incense as powder, perfuming, wearing, smearing, adorning, and donning all manner of ornaments,

garments, and accessories; not performing songs, dances, or theatrical performances, nor going to witness or listen to them— where "theatrical performances" refers to musical instruments, meaning that one does not personally practice singing, music, or dancing,
nor produce various forms of entertainment such as gambling with dice or chess, nor engage in such activities when performed by others.
At such times, one does not go to watch or listen [to performances]. Regarding "not sitting on high, wide, or large beds":
the height shall not exceed one chi and six cun; the width shall not exceed four chi; and the length shall not exceed eight chi.
Furthermore, one shall never sit or lie upon any bed or seat that is elaborately adorned or decorated. Regarding "not eating at improper times": this means not consuming food after midday.

Chewing the five grains, melons, fruits, and other such things—if the sun has passed the first meridian line until the sky has not yet dawned the following day—all this is termed "non-time" (*akāla*).
As the Sūtra says: "The devas eat in the morning; the Buddha eats at midday; animals eat when the sun sets;

ghosts and spirits eat at night. Now, by receiving the eight precepts and severing the causes for the six realms of existence, one studies the Buddha’s practice of eating at midday to manifest [this principle].

The Middle Way is that which avoids the faults of the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism. Once the meal is finished, one must chew a *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-stick) and rinse the mouth with pure water to remove residual saliva from within.
If one does not chew a *dantakāṣṭha* and swallows while residual saliva still remains in the mouth, one commits the offense of eating at an improper time (*vikālabhojana*).
If no tooth-stick is available—with the exception of poisonous trees—one may use any peach, *huai*, or bitter/astringent wood.
All [of these] may be used. As for the five pungent vegetables (*pañca-garaka*), one must not eat them at all.

Regarding these eight precepts of the fast (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*): if one violates the first four, it constitutes actual evil; they are natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). Drinking alcohol is the gateway to all evils.
The latter four are causes and conditions for negligence. If a person avoids the first five types of evil, this is a cause and condition for merit; avoiding the remaining four is likewise.
Regarding the causes and conditions of the Path, the *Bao’en jīng* (Sūtra on Requiting Kindness) states:

"If one violates a grave precept among the eight precepts, even if one subsequently receives the eight precepts again, or receives the five precepts, the ten precepts, the full ordination (*mahāśramaṇa-saṃvara*), the dhyāna-precepts, or the untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*), none of these will be obtained.
Question: Regarding the method for receiving the eight precepts, may they be received for two days, three days, or even up to ten days at once?
"May I receive it? He replied: "The Buddha originally established the precepts for one day and one night; they must not exceed this limit.

If one has the capacity to receive them, once one day has passed, one may receive them again in succession. In this way, according to the extent of one's capacity, one does not calculate by the number of days.

As for the method of receiving the *upavāsa* (fasting) rite, it must necessarily be received from another person; that is, one receives it from among the five assemblies (*pañca-saṃgha*). Thus, the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*..."
The *Śāstra* asks: "How is the eightfold precept of the one-day fast (upavāsa) obtained? It answers: "It is obtained through the instruction of another;

that is, through the teacher’s instruction, by personally making a sincere declaration and receiving it with reverence. Furthermore, the one who receives the precepts must follow the words of the teacher."
One receives the precepts only by speaking exactly as the preceptor speaks. If one speaks first oneself, or speaks simultaneously with the preceptor, the precepts are not received.
Question: What kind of clothing and ornaments must one wear to receive these precepts? Answer:
One may receive them while wearing whatever clothes and ornaments one habitually uses. However, if they are worn merely for temporary adornment of the body, one must...
It is abandoned. At the time of receiving it, it should last for exactly one day and night, neither more nor less;
that is, having received it from a teacher at dawn, this fast is abandoned by the following dawn. Question: If one receives this precept after noon, does one still obtain the precept? Answer:
One should say that one does not, except in the case of a prior commitment made every month on the sixth [day].

Those who regularly observe the fast and precepts may, due to other circumstances, fail to remember them before midday; however, if they only remember after having eaten, they should feel deep shame and remorse.
It is also permissible for them to then invite a preceptor and receive the precepts according to the Dharma. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"If there is absolutely no preceptor to confer the precepts, one may simply perform mental recollection and verbal declaration, taking refuge in the Triple Gem and saying: 'I uphold the eight precepts.'"

It is also not obtained. If there is a preceptor nearby, yet one gives rise to pride or indolence and does not go to receive the precepts from them, but instead receives them on one's own, one still does not obtain the precepts.
As the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "If one lacks reverence, the essence of the precepts is not generated;
if one receives them contrary to the Dharma, it merely produces wholesome conduct, but the essence of the precepts is not generated. Therefore, the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* says:
One must not receive the precepts before a Buddha image alone; one must receive them from another person.

It is pure in its fundamental basis, pure upon receiving, pure in its adornment, pure in its applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), pure in its mindfulness, and pure in its seeking of karmic reward. This is called the Dharma of the Three Refuges and the Pure Eightfold Precepts.
If one can take refuge and receive these eight precepts, with the exception of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*), all other [sins] are removed.

All evils shall be completely extinguished. If someone were to take the four great treasuries filled with the seven kinds of jewels and offer them as a gift to others, the merit thereof would not equal that of a person who observes the eight precepts for one day and one night, thereby attaining immeasurable retribution and reaching the bliss of Nirvana.
The *Saṃyukta-avadāna-sūtra* states: "Observing the fast for a single day..."
There are six hundred thousand years' worth of surplus grain; one does not eat at improper times. Furthermore, there are five blessings:
first, little illness; second, physical ease; third, little lust; fourth, little sleep; and fifth, rebirth in heaven with the knowledge of past lives. The *Śākyasūtra* states:
"On the six monthly fast days, if one observes the eight precepts, the merit is incalculable. If a person urgently desires to attain the holy fruit of the Three Vehicles..."
As for the Way, one should rectify the mind and unify the intention, receiving and upholding the eight precepts to obtain great and virtuous benefit.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If one receives and upholds these precepts from the first day to the fifteenth day of the twelfth lunar month, the merit thereof is greatest."
"This is the day when the Tathāgata manifests great supernormal powers. Furthermore, it is asked: "Between the five precepts and the one-day precepts (upavāsa), which is superior?

The answer is: "Due to specific causes and conditions, the two sets of precepts are equal. However, the five precepts are maintained for the duration of one's life, whereas the eight precepts are maintained for a single day.
Thus, while the five precepts are constant, they are few in number; the one-day precepts, though maintained for a shorter time," [are many in number].

However, the precepts are many. If one lacks the great resolve (*mahācitta*), then even if one maintains them for a lifetime, it is not equal to maintaining the eight precepts for a single day with that great resolve.
It is like a weakling who serves as a general; though he may wish to lead his troops for a lifetime, he will ultimately achieve neither merit nor fame.

If, however, a hero exerts himself, the chaos and disorder are immediately settled; the merit of a single day’s achievement brings renown that covers the whole world. The eight precepts are comparable to this.
It is likewise with the other precepts. Question: For what reason does one observe the eightfold precepts and cultivate merit for six days?
Answer: On these days, ghosts and spirits pursue people, seeking to snatch away their lives; they cause illness, misfortune, and decline, making people inauspicious.
Therefore, at the beginning of the kalpa, the sages and worthies taught people to observe the fast and cultivate merit in order to avoid such misfortunes. At that time...
They were unaware of the Eight Precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*), taking instead the mere abstention from food for one day as *poṣadha*.
After the Buddha appeared in the world, he first taught that one should observe the Eight Precepts for one day and one night, and that fasting after midday constitutes *poṣadha*.
Such merit leads a person to the bliss of Nirvāṇa. The *Caturmahārājakāyika-sūtra* states: "On the six *poṣadha* days of the month, the celestial messengers, the crown princes,"

The Four Heavenly Kings also descend from above to observe sentient beings. If there are none who practice generosity, uphold the precepts, or are loyal and filial, they ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to inform the Lord of Devas.
At that time, the Lord of Devas and all the devas are filled with displeasure in their hearts.
It is said: "The evil realms increase and the hosts of devas decrease.
Conversely, if there are many who practice giving, maintain the precepts, and are loyal and filial, the devas rejoice and say: "The hosts of devas increase and the evil realms diminish.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: The Buddha told the Great King, "In the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a butcher named Viśālakṣa."
Every day, he slaughtered countless sheep. Upon seeing Śāriputra, he immediately received the eight precepts for one day and one night.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, at the end of his life, he was reborn as a son of Virūḍhaka, the Heavenly King of the North.
The *Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish* states: In the kingdom of Avanti in Northern India, there was an old maidservant who was sent running on errands morning and night.
They find no place of rest; for even the slightest transgression, they are subjected to flogging and beating. Their clothing does not cover their bodies, and their food does not fill their mouths.
In their old age, they are exhausted and haggard; they long for death but cannot attain it. Carrying jars to the river to fetch water, they contemplate this suffering.
He raised his voice and wept bitterly. At that time, the Venerable Kātyāyana came to where he was and asked, "Why are you weeping and grieving so intensely?
He replied, "Venerable Sir, I am already advanced in years and must constantly perform arduous labor;
moreover, I am impoverished and lack sufficient food and clothing. I long for death but cannot obtain it; for this reason, I weep. The Venerable said, "If you..."
The poor woman asked, "Why not sell your poverty? The servant girl said, "How can poverty be sold? Who would buy poverty?
The Venerable One said, "Poverty can indeed be sold. This was repeated three times. The servant girl said, "If poverty can truly be sold, I ought to ask the method, Venerable Sir.
How is poverty to be sold? The Venerable One said, "If you truly wish to sell it, follow my words exactly. She replied, "Yes. The Venerable One—
The Venerable One said to him, "First, bathe. After he had bathed, the Venerable One said, "You should practice giving. He replied, "Venerable Sir, I am extremely poor and destitute;
I do not have even as much as my own hand to give. I have only this jar, which belongs to its owner. With what shall I give?
The Venerable One then took his alms bowl and gave it to him, saying, "Take this bowl, fetch a small amount of pure water, and [give it]."

He was instructed to fetch [the food] and present it to the Venerable One. Having accepted it, the Venerable One immediately offered a blessing. Next, he was instructed to receive the eightfold precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*).
Afterwards, he was taught to recollect the various merits of the Buddha. He asked, "Do you have a place to stay? He replied, "I do not.
When it was time to grind [grain], he would lie down where the grain was being ground. When there was work such as pounding rice or cooking, he would lie down right in the midst of it. Or...
At that time, there was no one at home; he stayed overnight on a heap of dung. The Venerable One said, "You must maintain a disciplined mind and perform your duties with reverence;
do not harbor resentment. He waited for himself until the master had finished sleeping everyone, then secretly opened the door from within a recess of the doorway.
She spread out pure grass for a seat, contemplated the Buddha, and resolved not to give rise to evil thoughts. At that time, the old maidservant followed the instructions and returned home;
acting according to her orders, she passed away during the latter part of the night and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
When the master rose early in the morning, he saw that the maidservant had died and said in anger, "This maidservant was never permitted to enter the house; why has she come this evening?"
Therefore, she died right there. Men were then made to bind her feet with grass ropes and drag her into the forest.
Since this woman had already been reborn in the heavens, she was enjoying herself with five hundred devaputras.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and asked, "By what merit have you been born in this heaven? She replied, "I do not know, Śāriputra."
He immediately lent his divine eye to observe the causes and conditions by which his former body had been reborn in heaven.
Due to Kātyāyana, five hundred devaputras then came to the forest, scattering flowers and burning incense to make offerings to the corpse.
The radiance of the devas’ bodies illuminated the village and the woods. When the host saw this, he marveled at its cause and went with the crowd to the forest to observe it.
Seeing the devaputras making offerings to this corpse, he asked the gods: "This maidservant was ugly and foul-smelling;
even while she was alive, people loathed the sight of her. Now that she is dead, for what reason do you devas offer her such worship?
At that time, the devaputra explained in detail the origins and the causes and conditions for her rebirth in heaven. He then returned to where Kātyāyana was, and said to the Venerable One: "For..."

The various devas and humans were extensively taught the sublime Dharma, namely the discourse on how observing the precepts leads to rebirth in heaven, that sensual desire is an impure dharma, and that renunciation is true happiness.
At that time, those devas and five hundred sons of gods attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* and flew back to their celestial palaces.
Then, the assembly gathered there, having heard the Dharma, each attained the fruits of the Path; there was none who did not rejoice and practice accordingly.

(Kātyāyana, he observed this maidservant with his divine eye and saw that she had but one night remaining of her life; upon death, she would fall into the evil realms and undergo immeasurable suffering.
Therefore, he went to deliver her. The *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra* says: "In the east there is a country named Uttara-pāṭha.

There were five hundred brahmins who, leading one another, wished to go to the banks of the Gaṅgā to perform sacrifices at the divine pool, bathe away their impurities, and seek immortality by going naked. On the way—
He emerged from a great marsh but became lost and could not pass through. Midway, he was exhausted of provisions.
Seeing a great tree in the distance that seemed to possess a divine aura, he imagined someone lived there. He hurried to gather under the tree, but saw nothing at all.

Raising his voice, he wept aloud, saying, "Starving and parched, beset by calamity, I shall die of exhaustion in this marsh. The tree spirit manifested its form and asked, "Where have you come from, O Daoist? Now..."
"What do you wish to do? they asked in unison. He replied, "I wish to go to the Divine Pond to bathe and seek immortality.
Today I am hungry and thirsty; I pray you will have pity on me and provide relief. The tree deity raised his hand, and food and drink of a hundred flavors flowed forth from it.

He provided food and drink for the multitude until all were fully satiated. There was enough of the remaining food and drink to serve as provisions for their journey. As they were about to part, he went before the deity to inquire further.
He asked, "What virtues did you practice in your former lives to attain such majestic stature? The deity replied, "In my past life, I resided in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a chief minister named Sudatta who provided meals for the Buddha and the assembly of monks. While purchasing curd in the marketplace, he found no one to carry it; he therefore requested me to carry it for him.
Upon arriving at the monastery, he had me serve the portions, and when it was finished, he gave me water for rinsing my hands. I remained there with solemn dignity."
They listened to the Dharma with everyone rejoicing and praising it immeasurably. At that time, I observed the fast; when I returned home in the evening, I did not eat.
My wife asked me in wonder, "I do not know what you are resentful about. I said, "I am not resentful. I saw the elder Sudatta providing a meal for the Buddha."
"I am observing the precepts and the fast; this fast is called the Eightfold Abstinence (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa). At that time, his wife spoke with anger and resentment, saying:

'Gautama disrupts the secular order; why should he be followed? You are destroying the traditional norms, and calamity will arise from this. Because she pressed him incessantly, they finally ate together."

At that time, my life-span having come to an end, my spirit was reborn here. Because this foolish woman broke my vow of purification (*upavāsa*) and prevented me from completing my practice, I have been reborn in this marsh as a tree deity.
By the merit of offering the curd, food and drink issue forth from my hands.
Had I fully observed the vow of purification, I should have been reborn in the heavens to enjoy natural abundance. Then, for the sake of five hundred people, he spoke these verses:

Sacrifices plant the roots of calamity; day and night they grow their branches and twigs. They cause bitter suffering and ruin the very foundation of the self. As for the Dharma-fast, it leads to the immortals who transcend the world.

According to the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* (*Xiányújīng*) and the *Sūtra of One Hundred Conditions* (*Bǎiyuánjīng*), after the parinirvāṇa of the former Buddha Kāśyapa, when his bequeathed Dharma was nearing its end, there were two brahmins who went to the bhikṣus and together received the eight precepts. One vowed to be reborn in heaven.

One wished to become a king; another who wished to be reborn in heaven returned home. His wife called out to him to eat together with her, but the husband said, "I have just received the Buddha’s fast-food offering;
I shall not eat after midday. The wife said, "You are a brahmin; you have your own system of precepts.
For what reason have you accepted the fast-food of a heterodox path? If you now go against this and do not eat with me, I shall report this matter to everyone."
"O Brahmin, you have been expelled and excluded from our assembly. Terrified by these words, he immediately ate at an improper time with his wife.

Because he had broken his fast, he was later reborn among the nāgas. As for the one who wished to become a king, because he had observed the fast perfectly, he was born into a royal family and became a great king.
At that time, there were many sweet fruits in the king’s garden, and the park keeper, every day...
I respectfully send this along. Later, that man found an extraordinary crabapple in the garden pond; its color and fragrance were most exquisite.
He then thought to himself, "Whenever I enter or exit, I am always stopped by the gatekeeper. I shall give this crabapple to him.
Once the gatekeeper had received it, he presented it as an offering to the eunuch. After the eunuch had accepted it, he passed it up to the lady. The lady...
He obtained a *nālikera* fruit and offered it again to the king. When the king ate this *nālikera*, he found it exceedingly sweet and delicious, and he questioned his consort.
Through successive inquiries, the matter was traced back to the garden keeper. The king summoned him immediately and rebuked him, saying, "Such a delicious *nālikera* as this—"
"Why did you not send it? You have instead given it to another! The gardener then related the matter from beginning to end. The King spoke in anger:
"From this day forward, you must always send these pomegranates. The garden supervisor informed the King: "These pomegranates have no seeds;
by what means can they be produced? The King said: "If you cannot obtain them, I shall have your head cut off. The man returned to the garden and raised his voice loudly.
He wept. Because the dragon’s previous life had observed the fast together with the King, it was born within a spring in the King’s garden.
At that time, the dragon transformed its body into human form, emerged from the spring, and asked the cause of his weeping. The garden keeper explained the situation in detail.
Upon hearing this, the dragon entered the water, brought forth a pomegranate placed in a golden platter, and sent it to be presented to the King, conveying its intention, saying: "I and..."
"O King, we were formerly close friends. In the past, when we were in the world, we were both brahmins who together observed the eight precepts, each seeking their own aspirations.
Your observance of the precepts was complete, so you have become a human king; my observance of the precepts was incomplete, so I was born among the nāgas.
Now I wish to receive the Eightfold Abstinence (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa) and seek to cast off this body. You should find for me the text of the Eightfold Abstinence and uphold it."
"Come and give it to me. If you do otherwise, I shall submerge your kingdom and turn it into a great ocean.

The garden overseer offered a *nāga-fruit* (*nai*) to the king and related the dragon’s intent in detail. Upon hearing this, the king was deeply distressed; for it was due to the fact that no Buddha existed in that age and the Dharma had already been extinguished that such texts for the ritual were difficult to find.
There was a high minister, to whom the king issued this command: "The dragon seeks the ritual methods for the fast; I rely upon you."
"If you do not obtain it, I shall kill you. The great minister returned home, filled with deep anxiety and distress.
When his father saw his son’s countenance was displeased, he questioned him and learned the full details. His father said to him, "The pillars in our hall constantly emit light;
try breaking one open and look inside—there must be something extraordinary. He immediately broke it open and found two volumes of scripture.
The scroll consisted of two parts: first, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination; second, the Text on the Eight Precepts of the Fast. Having obtained them, he presented them to the King.
The King was filled with joy and personally delivered them to the dragon. Upon receiving this scripture, the dragon presented the King with precious jewels in return.

Both the King and the dragon then redoubled their observance of the Eight Precepts. When their lives ended, they were reborn together in heaven. This continued until the appearance of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
They descended from heaven to the place where the Buddha was. The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and at that time both devaputras attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
They returned to the heavens, and from then on, they will ultimately attain *nirvāṇa*.

(According to this, these eight precepts may be received by anyone, whether they have already received the five precepts or not. On the six fast days, one’s own birthday, or the birthdays and memorial dates of one’s parents, they may be observed to support merit and wisdom and serve as the foundation for transcending the world.)

Furthermore, if after receiving the precepts one encounters circumstances that pressure one toward breaking them, it is better to renounce the precepts first and then act; thus one incurs no offense for violating the precepts and may receive them again later. When wishing to renounce the precepts, it does not matter whether one is a monastic or a layperson;

simply say to one person: "I now renounce the eight precepts and will not uphold them. Once this is said, the renunciation is accomplished. For further details, consult the *Guijie ji* (Collection on the Precepts of Taking Refuge).
During the reign of Sun Hao, King of Wu, he received the precepts from the śramaṇa Seng Kang.

In the first year of the Yongping era of Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty, the Emperor visited Huilin Garden and established the Eight Precepts Fast (bāguānzhāi). This was during the time when the Emperor was still of humble status.
He took refuge in the mountains of Jieyang and piled stones to construct a stupa. Suddenly, a tree grew beside it, shaped like a ceremonial canopy (*puṣpaka-vitāna*).
Later, when the Emperor fell ill, he issued an edict for various śramaṇas to pray to the Buddha for seven days; heavenly incense then filled the hall.

Emperor Wenxuan of the Qi dynasty ascended the throne through abdication and received the Bodhisattva precepts from Master Sengchou. Within the capital region, he prohibited the consumption of alcohol, the release of hawks, and the setting of nets;
furthermore, he banned slaughter throughout the empire on the six days of the fast during the first, fifth, and ninth months of each year.
He exhorted the people to observe the fasts and precepts, ensuring that all pungent and spicy foods were eliminated from both public and private life.
Emperor Wu, the Gaozu of the Liang dynasty, established the Guangzhai and Tongtai Temples, and throughout the realm, the six fast days and the eight precepts were universally observed.

Emperor Xiaozhuang of the Zhou dynasty greatly honored the Sun of the Buddha. He commissioned four niches for plain (unadorned) statues totaling over ten thousand figures and transcribed two thousand scrolls of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
He constantly propagated the practice of the six fast days and the eight precepts without interruption.
Emperor Jianwen, the Taizong of the Liang dynasty, established these two monasteries, Jing and Bao’en.
He drew his own blood to personally transcribe ten copies of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and vowed to observe a fast on the anniversary of [his parents'] deaths, abstaining from food.
Emperor Xiaowu of the Wei dynasty, whose personal name was Wen, held an Eight Precepts Fast at Zhongxing Temple on the anniversary of his birth.

When the midday meal was finished, his attendants Yuan Min, Sun, and others further presented fish and meat. The Emperor was enraged and demoted them all from their offices. He then issued an edict to dismiss the women of the six palaces.
All observed the three long fasts of the year and the monthly fast on the sixth day.

Chen’s Crown Prince Yuan, the successor to the throne, on the fifteenth day of the first month in the fourth year of Zhide (589 CE), held a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks at Chongzheng Hall and invited Master Zhiyi to bestow the Bodhisattva precepts upon him.
[Recorded in] *Bai lu qing jie* (The Hundred Records on Requesting the Precepts).
His style name was Yuan; according to the *Nan shi*, it was Shen. It is suspected that he changed this name upon requesting the bodhisattva precepts.
Emperor Wu of the Chen dynasty issued an edict summoning Master Zhizhe to the Chongzheng Hall to confer the bodhisattva precepts upon the Crown Prince.

During the tenth year of the Kaihuang era of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty, there was a drought. An imperial edict summoned Dharma Master Tanyan to lead the assembly in prayers for rain, but the rain did not fall.

The Emperor asked for the reason, and Tanyan replied, "The matter depends on two things. The Emperor dispatched Su Cheng, the Governor of the Capital, to inquire about the meaning of these two things.
Tanyan said, "Your Majesty personally manages the myriad affairs of state, while the various ministers exert the strength of their limbs as your aides."
Although they were both capable of governing the state, they equally failed in profound transformation; it was as if one wished for rain while the other withheld it—a matter of "one or two" factors.

The Emperor perceived their intent and commanded the relevant officials to select an auspicious day. He established the ceremonial rites in the main hall and invited [the Master] to ascend the imperial throne to receive the Eight Precepts.
Once the ministers had received them in succession, the air was as scorching as if on fire, yet a great rain poured down in torrents.
The Emperor was delighted. From then on, whenever Huiyan entered the court, the Emperor would invariably serve him with his own hands from the imperial table.

He issued an edict summoning Dharma Master Xing to the Taixing Palace to confer upon him the Bodhisattva Precepts. Furthermore, he decreed that throughout the empire, during the first, fifth, and ninth months, as well as the six days of the fast (*ṣaḍ-upoṣadha*), it shall be forbidden to kill living beings.
In the tenth month of winter, the thirteenth year of the Kaihuang era, the Great Master Zhi passed through Yuezhou and conferred the precepts upon the regional governor, Wang Xuanwu.
At the request of the śramaṇa Tanjie and others, he lectured on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*. Upon hearing the Dharma, the local populace was moved and transformed;
throughout the five counties of the prefecture, in more than one thousand locations, everyone abandoned fishing and hunting.
Prince Boyi of Chenyongyang, whose courtesy name was Cezhi, was the eighth son of Emperor Wen.

At the beginning of the Zhide era, he was appointed as the Regional Inspector of Dongyang and requested the Great Master Zhiyi to go there to preside over the lectures. After the Prince sent his letter three times, the Master finally went.
The King, his son Zhan, and their family members all received the Bodhisattva precepts together. By day they listened to the lectures, and by night they practiced seated meditation.
When the lecture series was about to conclude, he established a dharma-name for him called Jingzhi (Tranquil Wisdom).
During the reign of Emperor Jianwen of the Jin dynasty, a crow nested in the Taiji Hall. The Emperor summoned the nun Daorong and conferred upon her the Eight Precepts of the Fast;
the crow then carried its nest away.
When the Prince of Jin welcomed the Great Master Zhiyi to Yangzhou, he hosted a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks and conferred the Bodhisattva Precepts upon him.
Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty issued an edict for Dharma Master Chang to enter the inner palace to bestow the Bodhisattva precepts upon the Empress and the Crown Prince.

In the eleventh month of the first year of the Xianqing era, Empress Wu gave birth to the Crown Prince; a divine light filled the chamber, and he was granted the name Prince Foguang, who was later Emperor Zhongzong.
Over a month later, an edict was issued for Dharma Master Xuanzang to escort him to a monastery for ordination and the shaving of his hair.

[The Empress] received the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts. During the Zhongzong era, Emperor Zhongzong issued an edict for Vinaya Master Dao’an to enter the palace to confer the Refuges and Precepts upon the Consorts.
During the Xuanzong era, the Japanese monk Eiei arrived at Yangzhou and requested that Vinaya Master Jianzhen accompany him [to Japan].

He departed by ship. Upon arriving in Japan, the King welcomed him with hospitality and inquired after his well-being. He was lodged in the Vairocana Hall and requested the bestowal of the *śaraṇagamana* precepts;
thus did the Vinaya begin in Japan.
Minister Bai Juyi, whose courtesy name was Lètiān, styled himself the Layman of Mount Xiangshan.

He once exhorted one hundred and forty-eight people to form the "Assembly for Rebirth Above" at Bótà Temple, where they received the eightfold precepts nine times according to the teachings of Master Rù.

Phonetic Glossary: *Poṣadha* (布薩). This is translated as "Pure Abiding" (*jìngzhù*). It is also called "Heavenly Speech Pure Abiding. In human speech, it is sometimes called "Vigorous Progression" (*jīngjìn*) and also "Nurturing Growth" (*chángyǎng*).
It applies to both monastics and laypeople, who together undertake its practice. That is to say, it consists of purifying body, speech, and mind, in accordance with the precepts.
And they abide [in this].
Regarding the six days of fasting (*ṣaḍ-upoṣadha*), these refer to three days each in the first half of the month and the second half of the month.

The three days of the first half of the month are the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth; the three days of the second half of the month are the twenty-third, etc. (i.e., the twenty-fifth and the thirtieth). Thus it is said.
The eighth day of the first half of the month; the twenty-ninth and thirtieth days—namely, the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the first half of the month;
and the ten *zhāi* (fast) days: the first, the eighth, the fourteenth, the fifteenth, the eighteenth, the twenty-third, and the twenty-fourth.
Twenty-eight. Twenty-nine. Thirty. The month begins on the twenty-seventh day of the waning phase.
The five assemblies (*pañca-saṃgha*) are the five classes of those who have gone forth: first, the bhikṣu; second, the bhikṣuṇī; third, the śikṣamāṇā.
Fourth, śrāmaṇeras; fifth, śrāmaṇerīs.
Regarding the three evils and eight difficulties: the "three evils" refers to the three evil realms. As for the "eight difficulties," the first three are the three evil realms.

1. The four long-lived heavens (*dīrghāyuṣka-deva*), where the lifespan is five hundred *kalpas*; non-Buddhists who have attained the meditative absorption of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) are born there.
2. The continent of Uttarakuru. 3. Those who are blind, deaf, or mute. 4. Those with worldly wisdom and eloquence;

that is, those among worldly people who possess sharp and clever intellects but are addicted to heterodox texts and do not believe in the supramundane True Dharma. 5. Those born before or after the appearance of a Buddha.
Regarding these eight, because one is unable to see the Buddha or hear the Dharma in each case, they are called "difficulties.

There are four types of wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*): the gold-wheel king, whose transformative influence extends over the four continents; the silver-wheel king, whose governance excludes the northern continent of Uttarakuru;
the copper-wheel king, who excludes both the northern continent of Uttarakuru and the western continent of Aparagoyānī; and the iron-wheel [king].
O King, it is only in Jambudvīpa that these four wheel-turning kings appear.

As they are about to ascend the throne, a great precious wheel—manifested according to their respective merits—floats through the air to attend them. There are differences among them, consisting of gold, silver, copper, and iron; thus, there are four types.
The Brahma King dwells between the first and second dhyānas of the Rūpadhātu and presides over a small chiliocosm.
Regarding the four debts of gratitude: first, the debt to one's parents; second, the debt to sentient beings, meaning all sentient beings since beginningless kalpas.
Wandering through the six realms of rebirth over many lifetimes, beings have been each other’s parents. Fourth is the debt of gratitude to the Three Jewels;
the Three Jewels are a fertile field of merit, capable of enabling sentient beings to emerge from the suffering of birth and death and reach the bliss of nirvana.

The three realms of existence refer to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, so called because sentient beings therein undergo birth and death. The six heavens of the desire realm are:

first, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings; second, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; third, the Yāma Heaven; fourth, the Tuṣita Heaven; [fifth, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; and sixth, the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven].
Fifth, the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati); sixth, the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).
Regarding the realms of form and formlessness: the realm of form consists of the four dhyāna heavens; the realm of formlessness consists of the four spheres of emptiness.
The Śrāvakas cultivate the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths and realize the four fruits of the Hīnayāna.
The Pratyekabuddha— whose Sanskrit name is *Vaineyaka*,
with "vaina" sounding like "man"— is so called because he adorns his body and head with garlands of flowers strung together.

The five turbidities of the evil world: first, the turbidity of sentient beings, which refers to those sentient beings who do not fear the retribution of evil karma and do not cultivate wholesome dharmas;
second, the turbidity of views, which refers to the increase of false views and the failure to cultivate the path of goodness; third, the turbidity of afflictions.
This refers to sentient beings who have many desires and whose greed, hatred, and delusion are rampant, thereby distressing and confusing the mind and spirit.

Fourth is the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*), which means that human life expectancy decreases; those who live for a hundred years become rare because evil karma increases, and the duration of life becomes uncertain, falling to thirty, twenty, or ten years.
Fifth is the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), which refers to the three calamities: warfare, famine, and pestilence.
At the time of arising, sentient beings further kill and harm one another.
Kātyāyana is translated here as "Ornamentation" (Wénshì) and also as "Indeterminate.
The Sanskrit term for Bodhisattva is *bodhisattva*; people nowadays still abbreviate it, hence calling them "Bodhisattvas. *Bodhi*...
*Bodhi* means the Buddha-way. *Sattva* is translated here as "beings with great resolve," meaning those who enter the Buddha-way with a great resolve.
Furthermore, *sattva* is named "accomplishing beings," meaning that by means of the Buddha-way, one brings sentient beings to fulfillment.
*Srotāpanna* (須陀洹) here means "entering the stream," referring to one who has entered the stream of the noble ones (*ārya*).
This is the first fruit of sainthood. There are four fruits: first, *srotāpanna*; second, *sakṛdāgāmin* (斯陀含); third, *anāgāmin* (阿那含); and fourth, *arhat* (阿羅漢).
The five pungent vegetables are leek, garlic, chives, scallion, and asafoetida (*hingukhu*). *Jiu* is also a variety of leek; one must by no means consume them.
"Brahmacārin" is here translated as "Pure Conduct" (Jingxing), similar to the Confucian scholars of this land.
*Chuppu* (樗蒱): the first syllable is pronounced *shū* and the second *pú*; it refers to gambling games.

*Upāsaka* is here translated as "Male Lay Practitioner" (Jinshi Nan); *Upāsikā* is here translated as "Female Lay Practitioner" (Jinshi Nu), meaning one who has received the precepts of fasting (*upoṣadha*).
Only by observing the precepts can one draw near to and serve the Buddhas and noble ones. It is also called "near-dwelling" (*upavāsa*), meaning to dwell in proximity to the noble ones.
*Nirvāṇa* is here translated as "perfect quiescence," meaning that all virtues are fully perfected and karmic obstructions are eternally stilled; it is also called "non-arising."
It is not extinguished. Because it obstructs stillness, it neither arises nor ceases.

[The character 芼 (mào) has the departing tone; its pronunciation is jiào. It resembles an onion, but with a long stem and ridges. Among the five pungent vegetables, all those that are hollow inside belong to the onion category.
Some write it as 藠 (jiào), which is the name of a plant found on Mount Lú; it is not the same as 芼]. Some say:

As for *jiào* (leek), it is also of the same category as mountain leek (*shān-xiè*). This is not correct; it is [the plant known as] *jǐ* or *sī*. It is not recorded in the *Bencao* (Classic of Materia Medica); it is classified under the section for onions (*cōng*).
Therefore, they are not treated separately, nor are scallions recorded; this is because they lack functional utility.
